title: Values Filling Over a Third
statement:
You get an integer array nums of length n. Return every value that appears strictly more than ⌊n / 3⌋ times. Return each such value once, in any order. If there are none, return an empty list.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: n = 7, so a value needs more than 2 copies. Both 4 and 1 appear 3 times; [1, 4] is also accepted.
n = 6, so a value needs more than 2 copies. Each appears exactly twice, which is not enough.
n = 2, so ⌊n / 3⌋ = 0 and any value that appears at all qualifies.

hints: How many different values can each appear more than n/3 times? It is a small fixed number.
At most two. The classic majority vote keeps one candidate and a count; extend it to keep two.

When a value matches neither candidate and both counts are positive, cancel it against both: decrease both counts. Then count the two survivors in a second pass, because a survivor is only a candidate.

explain.intuition:
Three different values cannot each take more than a third of the array, so the answer has at most two values. That lets you keep just two candidates with a counter each.

The cancelling idea: whenever you see three different values (two candidates plus a newcomer that matches neither), throw all three away by decrementing both counters. Each such throw removes at most one copy of any true answer and removes three elements in total, so a value with more than n/3 copies cannot be cancelled out completely and must still be a candidate at the end. The converse is not true. A candidate may just be what was left, as in [1, 2, 3], so a second pass must count both candidates.
steps: Keep c1, n1 and c2, n2, two candidates with counts starting at 0.
For each x: if x == c1, increase n1. Else if x == c2, increase n2.
Else if n1 == 0, set c1 = x, n1 = 1. Else if n2 == 0, set c2 = x, n2 = 1.
Second pass: count the real occurrences of c1 and c2, and return those above ⌊n / 3⌋, without listing the same value twice.
pitfalls: Skipping the verification pass. In [1, 2, 3] both candidates survive, yet neither qualifies.
Checking the empty slots before the matches. If x equals c2 but n1 is 0, you would wrongly start a second copy of the same value in slot 1.
Using ≥ n/3 instead of strictly more than ⌊n / 3⌋. In [5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7] nobody qualifies.

solutions.title: Count each value separately
solutions.idea: For every element, count how many times it appears in the whole array.

solutions.title: Hash map of counts
solutions.idea: Count every value once, then keep the ones above the threshold.

solutions.title: Two-candidate vote
solutions.idea: Cancel triples of different values, keep two candidates, then verify them.

followups: Generalise to every value appearing more than n/k times. How many candidates do you need?
The numbers arrive as a stream too large to store. Can you still answer, and what changes about the second pass?
